prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT delay empiric antimicrobial therapy while awaiting imaging or LP results when bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected.

Do not delay lumbar puncture or antibiotics to obtain a CT head: cranial imaging is not routine before lumbar puncture (WHO 2025 section A.4; NICE NG240 1.4.6) and no imaging-first criterion is present.
Do NOT rely on a negative Gram stain or a 'normal CT' to rule out bacterial meningitis when the clinical syndrome is present.
Do NOT treat with oral antibiotics alone; CNS penetration is inadequate for meningitis.
required_recommendations: Give ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours (or cefotaxime 2 g IV every 6 hours) within 60 minutes of clinical suspicion, after blood cultures and without waiting for imaging or lumbar puncture (WHO 2025, strong recommendation; NICE NG240 1.4.1 and 1.6.3). Add vancomycin only where pneumococcal resistance to penicillin or third-generation cephalosporins is highly prevalent locally (WHO 2025, conditional recommendation).

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified, and stop it once another organism is identified (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3). Continue for 4 days: Streptococcus pneumoniae is identified.
Draw two sets of peripheral blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose.

Proceed to lumbar puncture without prior cranial imaging: no WHO 2025 section A.4 criterion is present (GCS 14, no focal signs, no cranial nerve deficit, no papilledema, no new seizure, no known severe immunocompromise at presentation). Age, confusion and diabetes are not imaging criteria.
Send full CSF panel (cell count, differential, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, meningitis multiplex PCR, lactate) at the LP.

Narrow therapy once the organism and susceptibilities are known: S. pneumoniae resistant to penicillin at meningitis breakpoints (MIC 0.12 mg/L) and susceptible to ceftriaxone (MIC 0.5 mg/L or less), so continue ceftriaxone, stop any vancomycin, and do not switch to penicillin or amoxicillin.
Place patient on droplet precautions until meningococcal disease is excluded.

Refer to clinical immunology to confirm suspected common variable immunodeficiency (IgG 185 mg/dL with low IgA and IgM; serotype-specific pneumococcal antibody results pending) after excluding secondary causes of hypogammaglobulinemia, and plan immunoglobulin replacement therapy.
Arrange formal audiological assessment before discharge, or within 4 weeks of discharge if it cannot be done before (WHO 2025, strong recommendation).

avoided_actions.rationale: No evidence of endocarditis as a primary source in this case; echocardiography is not part of routine meningitis workup.
No arrhythmia indication; continuous cardiac monitoring contributes nothing to meningitis diagnosis or treatment.
PET imaging has no role in acute meningitis diagnosis; CT and MRI cover the indications.
Amyloid PET is a dementia biomarker tool with no role in acute infectious meningitis.

CT before lumbar puncture is not indicated: no WHO 2025 section A.4 criterion is present (GCS 14, no focal signs, no cranial nerve deficit, no papilledema, no new seizure, no known severe immunocompromise at presentation). Imaging here only delays the lumbar puncture.

accepted: Acute bacterial meningitis due to Streptococcus pneumoniae in undiagnosed Common Variable Immunodeficiency

differential.key_features: Raised by the clear CSF with mixed pleocytosis and negative Gram stain; excluded by glucose ratio 0.35, protein 78 mg/dL, lactate 3.8 mmol/L and S. pneumoniae on multiplex PCR with no viral target detected.
Excluded: HSV PCR negative, no seizures or focal deficits, bacterial organism identified.
Raised by nasal congestion and frontal headache attributed to sinusitis; excluded as the sole diagnosis by neck stiffness, confusion and a CSF pleocytosis with S. pneumoniae on PCR.
Against: 2-day course, no TB exposure, S. pneumoniae identified in CSF and blood.
Raised by the immunodeficiency; excluded by negative CSF cryptococcal antigen and no Cryptococcus on the panel.

key_clinical_evidence: Acute bacterial meningitis presents with fever, headache, meningismus, and altered mental status; the full triad is present in only ~40%, so partial syndromes warrant aggressive workup.
Antibiotics are given within 60 minutes of suspicion; neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay them (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.4.1).

Proceed to lumbar puncture without prior cranial imaging: no WHO 2025 section A.4 criterion is present (GCS 14, no focal signs, no cranial nerve deficit, no papilledema, no new seizure, no known severe immunocompromise at presentation). Age, confusion and diabetes are not imaging criteria.

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified, and stop it once another organism is identified (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3).

A negative Gram stain does not exclude bacterial meningitis: sensitivity is about 85% with wide confidence limits (WHO 2025), lower after antibiotics; culture and multiplex PCR establish the organism.
A CSF:blood glucose ratio of 0.4 or less is abnormally low (WHO 2025 A.2.2) and is more informative than the absolute value, above all in hyperglycemia.

Empirical therapy is ceftriaxone or cefotaxime within 60 minutes, with ampicillin when a Listeria risk factor (age over 60, pregnancy, immunocompromise) is present; vancomycin only where pneumococcal resistance is locally prevalent (WHO 2025).

Prior oral antibiotics can lower the CSF cell count, shift the differential toward lymphocytes and sterilize the Gram stain and culture; the glucose ratio, protein, lactate and multiplex PCR are less affected.

Recurrent infections with encapsulated bacteria (sinopulmonary infections, otitis media, pneumococcal pneumonia, bronchiectasis) and a failed pneumococcal vaccine response in an adult point to a primary antibody deficiency such as common variable immunodeficiency.

metadata.condition_name: Acute bacterial meningitis (Streptococcus pneumoniae) with underlying Common Variable Immunodeficiency
metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle: presentation is masked by 5 days of prior oral antibiotic treatment, producing clear CSF with mixed pleocytosis and negative gram stain that initially mimics viral meningitis. The patient has only a low-grade temperature in the ED (37.8 degrees Celsius on acetaminophen), has only mild neck stiffness with equivocal meningeal signs, and a primary-care attribution of the headache to sinusitis provides an alternative explanation for symptoms. The critical clues — elevated CSF lactate, low glucose ratio, and the clinical pattern of recurrent encapsulated organism infections pointing to CVID — require careful integration across multiple data sources.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 4 required actions (labs, blood cultures, CSF, immunoglobulins); 3 red herrings; partial oral antibiotic treatment produces a muted, mixed CSF response
metadata.revision_reason: Reviewer 2 meningitis audit: complete LP/microbiology/lab pathway, no ECG, and MRI restricted to complications or non-response

patient.history_present_illness:
A 49-year-old woman who works as a childminder presents to the emergency department with a 2-day history of progressive headache and neck stiffness, with new confusion noticed by her husband earlier today. She has a well-documented 2-year history of recurrent upper and lower respiratory tract infections, including multiple episodes of otitis media and one hospitalization for pneumococcal pneumonia three months ago. She was previously diagnosed with adult-onset asthma based on wheezing episodes, though her pulmonary function tests reportedly showed no bronchodilator reversibility, and a subsequent workup revealed low exhaled nitric oxide and no eosinophilia, casting doubt on the asthma diagnosis. Bronchiectasis was noted on imaging six months ago. She received pneumococcal vaccination one year ago but continued to develop infections at the same frequency.

Five days prior to presentation, she developed nasal congestion, productive cough, and low-grade fevers, for which her primary care physician prescribed amoxicillin-clavulanate empirically. Over the subsequent three days, she noted progressive frontal headache initially attributed to sinusitis. Two days ago, she developed posterior neck stiffness which she attributed to sleeping in an awkward position. She took acetaminophen with partial relief. Earlier today, her husband noted she seemed more confused than usual, had difficulty following conversations, and was slower in her responses. She reported mild nausea without vomiting and subjective fevers at home, though her measured temperature was only 37.4 degrees Celsius with acetaminophen on board. She denies seizures, focal weakness, visual changes, or rash. She had no recent travel, no sick contacts beyond the children at her daycare, and no known exposure to tuberculosis. She denies any prior neurological symptoms. She presents to the ED tonight after her husband became concerned about her increasing lethargy and confusion.

neurological_exam.additional: Mild neck stiffness on passive flexion; Kernig sign equivocal (patient reports posterior thigh tightness but unclear if this represents true meningismus or musculoskeletal discomfort). Brudzinski sign negative. No papilledema on fundoscopic exam. Mild conjunctival injection bilaterally. Bilateral coarse crackles at lung bases on auscultation. Mild splenomegaly on palpation.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin performed normally without dysmetria bilaterally.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, reactive to light 3mm bilaterally. Visual fields full to confrontation. Extraocular movements intact without nystagmus. No facial asymmetry. Mild photophobia reported but does not withdraw to penlight. Hearing grossly intact. Palate elevates symmetrically. Tongue midline. No dysarthria.
neurological_exam.gait: Not formally tested; patient reports mild unsteadiness when standing, attributes it to headache and malaise.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert but appears fatigued and mildly irritable. Oriented to person and place, but initially states the date incorrectly by one day. GCS 14 (E4, V4, M6). Attention mildly impaired on serial 7s (4/5 correct). Short-term recall 2/3 objects at 5 minutes.
neurological_exam.motor: Strength 5/5 in all extremities. No pronator drift. Normal bulk and tone throughout.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric in biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, patellar, and Achilles tendons bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch and pinprick sensation intact and symmetric in all extremities. Proprioception intact at great toes bilaterally.
